## The group

Rathmines Library, the meeting room upstairs, last Thursday of the month at 7pm. This round: Bríd Nolan (retired nurse, sharpest reader in the room), Tadhg Ó Briain (accountant, arrived a sceptic and stayed one), Inés Carvalho (Portuguese, works in the tech sector on Barrow Street), Seán Fahy (retired Garda), and me. Bríd chose Marcus Aurelius for autumn 2024 and we gave it four meetings.

## Which translation

Argued about this for the first 20 minutes of the first meeting. In the room:

- Gregory Hays (Modern Library, 2002). Plain modern English. Bríd, Inés and me.
- Martin Hammond (Penguin Classics, 2006). More literal, very good notes. Tadhg.
- Meric Casaubon's 1634 version, the first in English, which Seán found in a charity shop on Camden Street for €3 and read out in a voice.

Decision: use Hays for quoting, check Hammond when a sentence matters. The page numbers below are Hays.

## 26 September 2024: Books I and II

Book I is the list of debts: what he learnt from his grandfather, his mother, his teachers, Antoninus. Tadhg found it smug; Bríd found it the most moving thing in the book, a man thanking people by name for what they taught him. Book I closes "Among the Quadi, on the Gran". He wrote much of it on campaign on the Danube in the Marcomannic wars, in Greek, for himself. The title we use was given later; the manuscripts call it something like *To Himself*.

Book II.1, p. 17, the morning one: "When you wake up in the morning, tell yourself: the people I deal with today will be meddling, ungrateful, arrogant..." Seán said that was every shift he ever did.

## 31 October 2024: Books III to V

The big one for me was IV.3, p. 38: people seek retreats in the country, at the sea, in the hills, "but nowhere you can go is more peaceful than your own mind". Inés pushed back: easy to say if you are emperor and someone else does the cooking. Good point, never fully answered.

Also V.1, the "why should I get out of bed" passage. Unanimous favourite.

## 28 November 2024: Books VI to VIII

Mood darker. The plague in the background (the Antonine plague from 165 AD, probably smallpox). VI.13: describing roast meat as a dead animal, wine as grape juice, sex as friction. Tadhg: "So he's a killjoy." Bríd: "He's trying to see things as they are." We moved to the pub for the last half hour.

December skipped, Christmas.

## 30 January 2025: Books IX to XII and verdict

Bríd asked the question nobody could answer: if the philosophy was so good, why did he make his son Commodus emperor? Inés: because a philosophy for living isn't a philosophy for choosing successors. Seán: because he was a father.

Scores out of 10:

| Member | Score |
|---|---|
| Bríd | 9 |
| Inés | 7 |
| Me | 8 |
| Seán | 7 |
| Tadhg | 4 |

## What I took from it

Reading the book together is a different thing from trying to live by it. The group argued, the morning exercises I do alone are another matter; see [[Stoicism daily practice]]. The book club made me see Marcus as a tired man on a frontier, at the end of the long [[Roman roads]] that led out from Rome, not as a life coach.
